### 4.6.1 – Review of Inequalities

* Inequalities compare two quantities.
  Examples:

  * (x > 3) means “x is greater than 3.”
  * (y \le 5) means “y is less than or equal to 5.”
* On a number line:

  * Open circle → (>) or (<)
  * Closed circle → (\ge) or (\le)

:::{.you-try title="Review One-Variable Graphs"}
Graph (x < -2) and (x \ge 4) on a number line.
Which parts are shaded?
:::

---

### 4.6.2 – Linear Inequalities in Two Variables

A **linear inequality** looks like a linear equation, but it uses an inequality symbol instead of an equals sign.

Examples:
[
y > 2x + 1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad y \le -x + 4
]

Each inequality represents **many points** that make the statement true — not just one line.

:::{.remember title="Boundary Line Rules"}

* Use a **dashed line** for (<) or (>).
* Use a **solid line** for (\le) or (\ge).
:::

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/inequality_boundary_line.png){width="360px" fig-align="center"}

---

### 4.6.3 – Shading the Solution Region

1. Graph the boundary line for the related equation ((y = mx + b)).
2. Choose a **test point** (often (0, 0)) and plug it into the inequality.
3. If it makes the statement true, shade that side of the line.

:::{.example title="Example – (y > x + 1)"}

1. Graph (y = x + 1) as a **dashed line**.
2. Test (0, 0): (0 > 0 + 1) → (0 > 1) is **false**.
   So shade the **other side** of the line.
:::

:::{.you-try title="Try It"}
Graph (y \le -2x + 3).
Use (0, 0) to decide where to shade.
:::

---

### 4.6.4 – Interpreting the Shaded Region

The shaded area shows **all the possible solutions** that make the inequality true.

:::{.real-world title="Example – Budget Constraint"}
You’re buying pens for $2 each and notebooks for $3 each.
You can spend at most $18.
[
2x + 3y \le 18
]

* The line (2x + 3y = 18) is the spending limit.
* The shaded region below it shows **all combinations** you can afford.
:::

:::{.think title="Why Shade Below?"}
“Less than or equal to” means you’re staying **under** the limit — so shade **below** the line.
:::

:::{.you-try-m title="Try Your Own"}
Write and graph an inequality to model this:
“You can drive up to 300 miles on 15 gallons of gas.”
:::

:::{.connect title="Where Both Conditions Are True"}
If you graph two inequalities at once, the **overlapping shaded region**  
shows where **both** are true — just like the point of intersection for two lines.  
Those shared values are the **solutions** to the system.
:::

---

:::{.remember title="Key Idea"}
Linear inequalities show **ranges of solutions** rather than exact ones.
The boundary line shows where values are equal, and the shading shows where the inequality is true.
:::
